Tafsir of Surat al-Mursalat

It is Makki according to the majority of the exegetes. Al-Naqqash related that it was said that among it is something Madani: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48], on the interpretation of one who said that it is a narration about the state of the hypocrites, and that it is in the sense of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And they are called to prostration, but they are not able﴾ [al-Qalam: 42]. Ibn Mas'ud said: This surah was revealed while we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Khaybar... the hadith in full.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿By those sent forth successively﴾ ﴿and those that blow with violence﴾ ﴿and those that spread [rain] widely﴾ ﴿and those that separate [by] distinguishing﴾ ﴿and those that deliver a reminder﴾ ﴿as excuse or warning﴾ ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is to occur.﴾ ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾ ﴿and when the sky is split open﴾ ﴿and when the mountains are blown away﴾ ﴿and when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾ ﴿For what day have they been postponed?﴾ ﴿For the Day of Judgment.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what is the Day of Judgment?﴾ ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers.﴾

Many of the exegetes said: "al-Mursalat" refers to the messengers sent to people from among the prophets, peace be upon them, as if He, Exalted is He, said: "And the sent groups." Abu Salih, Muqatil, and Ibn Mas'ud said: "al-Mursalat" are the angels sent with revelation and with successive descent upon the servants at the two ends of the day. Ibn Mas'ud also said, as did Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada: "al-Mursalat" are the winds. Al-Hasan ibn Abi'l-Hasan said: "al-Mursalat" are the clouds. The meaning of "'urfan" according to the first view is: "'urfan" from Allah and bounty upon His servants through the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Whoever does good will not lack one who repays him; kindness does not vanish between Allah and the people."

It may be that by His saying "'urfan" He intends "successive," by way of comparison with the successiveness of the mane of a horse and the ridges of mountains and the like. The Arabs say: "The people are one 'urf toward so-and-so" when they turn toward him. It may also be that He intends: "with the 'urf," i.e., with the truth and the command to good. These statements about "'urfan" fit the view of one who says that "al-Mursalat" are the angels. As for one who says that "al-Mursalat" are the winds, the interpretation of "al-'urf" fits as the specification of the winds which are a blessing, by which provisions and deliverance at sea come about, and other things that contain no punishment; and the other kind of wind would be in His saying, Exalted is He, "and those that blow with violence." It may be that "'urfan" means: and the winds that people recognize and are accustomed to, then He follows it with mention of the disapproved, harmful kind, which is "those that blow with violence." It may also be that by "'urf" He intends the successiveness of the winds, like the mane of a horse and the like; and the Arabs say: "A successive wind has blown." The statement about "'urf" with "al-Mursalat" being the winds applies equally if "al-Mursalat" are the clouds. 'Isa read "'urfa" with a damma on the ra'.

"Al-'asif" is the strong wind that uproots trees and other things.

The people differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: "and those that spread." Muqatil and al-Suddi said: they are the angels who spread the scrolls of the servants with their deeds. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatada said: they are the winds that spread Allah's mercy and rain. Some interpreters said: "al-Nashirat" are the groups of angels who directly bring the dead out of their graves for resurrection, as if they give them life. Some people said: "al-Nashirat" are the decayed bones at the resurrection on the Day of Judgment; it is said: "the dead person was resurrected (nashara)," and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"...... *** O wonder at the resurrected dead!"

It was also said: "al-Nashirat" are the lands that come to life by the rains, likened to a dead person who is raised. Abu Salih said: "al-Nashirat" are the rains that give life to the earth.

"Al-Fariqat": Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Salih, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said: they are the angels who distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful. Qatada, al-Hasan, and Ibn Kaysan said: "al-Fariqat" are the verses of the Qur'an.

As for "al-Mulqiyat dhikran," according to the view of the majority they are the angels; Muqatil said: Jibril, peace be upon him, and the like. Others said: they are the messengers, peace be upon them. The majority of readers recited "fa'l-mulqiyat" with the lam sukun, meaning they convey it from Allah, Exalted is He, and by His command, to the messengers, peace be upon them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, according to what al-Mahdawi mentioned, recited "fa'l-mulqiyat" with a fatha on the lam, a fatha on the qaf and its shadda, meaning they receive it from the side of Allah, Exalted is He. Ibn 'Abbas also recited "fa'l-mulqiyat" with a fatha on the lam, a shadda on the qaf and a kasra, meaning: they convey it to the messengers, peace be upon them. "Al-Dhikr" means the books, the laws, and their contents.

The readers differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿'Udhran aw nudhran﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read with sukun on the dhal in "'udhran" and damma in "nudhran." Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim, and Ibrahim al-Taymi read with sukun on the dhal in both. Talha, 'Isa, al-Hasan (with variation), Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, and al-A'mash from Ibn Kathir from 'Asim read with damma in both. The sukun on the dhal is on the basis that both are verbal nouns (masadir), as one says "'udr" and "'udhir," "nudhr" and "nadhir," like "nakir" and "nukr." The damma on the dhal is also valid with the sense of verbal nouns, and it may be the plural of "nadhir" and "'adhir," which are active participles; the meaning being that the remembrance is conveyed with excuse and warning, or that it is conveyed by those who excuse and warn. As for the accusative in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿'udhran aw nudhran﴾, if both are verbal nouns it may be a substitution (badal) for "al-dhikr"; it may also be an object of "al-dhikr," as if He, Exalted is He, said: "fa'l-mulqiyat an yudhkara 'udhran"; and "'udhran" may be an object of purpose, i.e., they convey the remembrance for the sake of excusing. If "'udhran aw nudhran" is plural, the accusative is a state (hal). Ibrahim al-Taymi read: "'udhran wa nudhran" with waw in place of "aw."

His saying, Exalted is He: "Indeed, what you are promised is to occur." This is what the oath is made upon, and an allusion to the resurrection. "Tams al-nujum" is the removal of their light and their leveling with the rest of the body of the sky. "Farij al-sama'" is its cleaving until openings appear in it. "Nasf al-jibal" is after their being set in motion; it was also said that it is their becoming dust, which is their scattering by the wind. The majority read "uqqitat" with a hamza and shadda on the qaf; 'Isa and Khalid read with the qaf light with the hamza. Abu 'Amr alone read "wuqqitat" with a waw, and Abu al-Ashhab, 'Isa, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read it likewise. 'Isa said: it is a lower dialect of Mudar. Abu Ja'far read with a single light waw and light qaf, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan. Al-Hasan ibn Abi'l-Hasan read "wawuqqitat" with two waws, on the pattern of "fawa'alat"; the meaning being: a set time was made for them, so it came and arrived. The waw in all of this is the original and the hamza is a substitution.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿li-ayyi yawmin ujjilat﴾ is an expression of wonder and a glorification of the greatness and awfulness of that day. Then He, Exalted is He, explained what He wondered about with His saying: "li-yawm al-fasl," meaning: the separation among creatures in their disputes, their reckoning, and their stations, whether to Paradise or to Hell. From this verse the judges derived the deferment of terms in litigation so that the decisive judgment occurs when they are complete. Then He, glorified be He, magnified the Day of Judgment by His saying: "wa-ma adraka ma yawmu'l-fasl," in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-ma adraka ma al-haqqah" and other similar verses. Then He, Exalted is He, affirmed woe for the deniers on that day; the meaning being: for those who denied it in this world and all the divisions of the Law. "Al-Waył" is war and sorrow over calamities that befall a person. It is related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, Ibn Mas'ud, and 'Ammar ibn Yasir that a valley in Hell is named al-Waył.

The meaning of "'urfan" according to the first view is: "'urfan" from Allah and bounty upon His servants through the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, and from it is the saying of the poet:

The meaning of "'urfan" according to the first view is: "'urfan" from Allah and bounty upon His servants through the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them, and from it is the saying of the poet:

Some people said: "al-Nashirat" are the decayed bones at the resurrection on the Day of Judgment; it is said: "the dead person was resurrected (nashara)," and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"...... *** O wonder at the resurrected dead!"

It was also said: "al-Nashirat" are the lands that come to life by the rains, likened to a dead person who is raised. Abu Salih said: "al-Nashirat" are the rains that give life to the earth.

"Al-Fariqat": Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Salih, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said: they are the angels who distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful. Qatada, al-Hasan, and Ibn Kaysan said: "al-Fariqat" are the verses of the Qur'an.

As for "al-Mulqiyat dhikran," according to the view of the majority they are the angels; Muqatil said: Jibril, peace be upon him, and the like. Others said: they are the messengers, peace be upon them. The majority of readers recited "fa'l-mulqiyat" with the lam sukun, meaning they convey it from Allah, Exalted is He, and by His command, to the messengers, peace be upon them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, according to what al-Mahdawi mentioned, recited "fa'l-mulqiyat" with a fatha on the lam, a fatha on the qaf and its shadda, meaning they receive it from the side of Allah, Exalted is He. Ibn 'Abbas also recited "fa'l-mulqiyat" with a fatha on the lam, a shadda on the qaf and a kasra, meaning: they convey it to the messengers, peace be upon them. "Al-Dhikr" means the books, the laws, and their contents.

The readers differed concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿'Udhran aw nudhran﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read with sukun on the dhal in "'udhran" and damma in "nudhran." Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim, and Ibrahim al-Taymi read with sukun on the dhal in both. Talha, 'Isa, al-Hasan (with variation), Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywa, and al-A'mash from Ibn Kathir from 'Asim read with damma in both. The sukun on the dhal is on the basis that both are verbal nouns (masadir), as one says "'udr" and "'udhir," "nudhr" and "nadhir," like "nakir" and "nukr." The damma on the dhal is also valid with the sense of verbal nouns, and it may be the plural of "nadhir" and "'adhir," which are active participles; the meaning being that the remembrance is conveyed with excuse and warning, or that it is conveyed by those who excuse and warn. As for the accusative in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿'udhran aw nudhran﴾, if both are verbal nouns it may be a substitution (badal) for "al-dhikr"; it may also be an object of "al-dhikr," as if He, Exalted is He, said: "fa'l-mulqiyat an yudhkara 'udhran"; and "'udhran" may be an object of purpose, i.e., they convey the remembrance for the sake of excusing. If "'udhran aw nudhran" is plural, the accusative is a state (hal). Ibrahim al-Taymi read: "'udhran wa nudhran" with waw in place of "aw."

His saying, Exalted is He: "Indeed, what you are promised is to occur." This is what the oath is made upon, and an allusion to the resurrection. "Tams al-nujum" is the removal of their light and their leveling with the rest of the body of the sky. "Farij al-sama'" is its cleaving until openings appear in it. "Nasf al-jibal" is after their being set in motion; it was also said that it is their becoming dust, which is their scattering by the wind. The majority read "uqqitat" with a hamza and shadda on the qaf; 'Isa and Khalid read with the qaf light with the hamza. Abu 'Amr alone read "wuqqitat" with a waw, and Abu al-Ashhab, 'Isa, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read it likewise. 'Isa said: it is a lower dialect of Mudar. Abu Ja'far read with a single light waw and light qaf, which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan. Al-Hasan ibn Abi'l-Hasan read "wawuqqitat" with two waws, on the pattern of "fawa'alat"; the meaning being: a set time was made for them, so it came and arrived. The waw in all of this is the original and the hamza is a substitution.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿li-ayyi yawmin ujjilat﴾ is an expression of wonder and a glorification of the greatness and awfulness of that day. Then He, Exalted is He, explained what He wondered about with His saying: "li-yawm al-fasl," meaning: the separation among creatures in their disputes, their reckoning, and their stations, whether to Paradise or to Hell. From this verse the judges derived the deferment of terms in litigation so that the decisive judgment occurs when they are complete. Then He, glorified be He, magnified the Day of Judgment by His saying: "wa-ma adraka ma yawmu'l-fasl," in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-ma adraka ma al-haqqah" and other similar verses. Then He, Exalted is He, affirmed woe for the deniers on that day; the meaning being: for those who denied it in this world and all the divisions of the Law. "Al-Waył" is war and sorrow over calamities that befall a person. It is related from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, Ibn Mas'ud, and 'Ammar ibn Yasir that a valley in Hell is named al-Waył.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 77, verse 16–28:

(p-505) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ ﴿Then We follow them with the later ones.﴾ ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals.﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Did We not create you from a despised fluid?﴾ ﴿Then We placed it in a secure lodging,﴾ ﴿for a known term.﴾ ﴿So We determined it, and how excellent are the determiners!﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle,﴾ ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains, lofty, and gave you to drink sweet water.﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾

The majority of reciters read "thumma nutbi'uhum" (then We follow them) with a damma on the 'ayn, as a new statement. Abu 'Amr, as related from him, read "thumma nutbi'hum" with a jazm on the 'ayn, as a conjunction with "nuhlik" (We destroy). This is the reading of al-A'raj. According to these two readings, the interpretation of "al-awwalin" (the former ones) differs. Whoever reads the first makes "al-awwalin" the nations that preceded Quraysh altogether, and then Allah, exalted is He, informs that He will follow "al-akhirin" (the later ones), meaning Quraysh, with the conduct of those (earlier nations) if they disbelieve and take their path. Whoever reads the second makes "al-awwalin" the people of Noah and Abraham and those who were with them, and "al-akhirin" the people of Pharaoh and everyone who came after and near the period of Muhammad (ﷺ). In the codex of 'Abdullah, the reading is "wa-sanutbi'uhum" (and We shall follow them). Then He, exalted is He, said: "Thus do We deal with the criminals," meaning in the future, so Quraysh and others among the disbelievers enter here.

As for the repetition of His saying in this surah: "Woe on that Day to the deniers," it has been said that it is merely for emphasis. It has also been said that rather, each verse of it contains something that calls for belief, so the threat upon denial comes to confirm what is in the verse.

Then He, exalted is He, pointed to the origin of creation, the consideration of which necessitates the possibility of resurrection. "Al-ma' al-mahin" (the despised fluid) means the weak one, namely the semen of the man and the woman. "Al-qarar al-makin" (the secure lodging) is the womb and the belly of the woman. "Al-qadr al-ma'lum" (the known term) is the time of birth; its meaning is known to Allah, exalted is He, in each individual person, whereas for human beings it differs, so the specific term of a particular person is not known to them. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Nafi', and al-Kisa'i read "faqaddarna" with a shaddah on the dal, while the rest read it without the shaddah. Both have the same meaning, from qudra (power) and qadr (decree), and from taqdir (determination) and tawqif (fixing). His saying, exalted is He, "al-qadirun" (the determiners) favours the reading of the majority. As for Ibn Mas'ud, he related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he explained "al-qadirin" as "al-muqaddirin" (those who determine). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "faqaddarna" with a shaddah on the dal, "fa-ni'ma al-muqtadirun" (and how excellent are those who are capable).

"Al-kifat" means a covering and a vessel that gathers a thing, by consensus. You say: "kafata al-rajula sha'rahu" when he gathers his hair with a cloth. So the earth gathers the living upon its back and gathers the dead in its belly. "Ahya'an" (for the living), according to this interpretation, is governed by His saying, glorified is He, "kifatan," because it is a verbal noun. Some of those who interpreted said that "ahya'an wa-amwatan" means only that the earth contains regions of living things and regions of dead things, meaning what grows and what does not grow; the accusative of "ahya'an" in this case is then a circumstantial state (hal) of "al-ard" (the earth). The first interpretation is stronger. Banan said: "We went out with al-Sha'bi to a funeral, and he looked at the graveyard and said: 'This is the kifat of the dead.' Then he looked at the houses and said: 'This is the kifat of the living.'" The Arabs used to call "Baqi' al-Gharqad" a "kafta," because it is a cemetery that gathers the dead. In a hadith: "Cover your vessels, tie the mouths of your waterskins, gather in your children (ikfitu sibyanakum), close your doors and extinguish your lamps." Ibn Mas'ud buried a louse in the mosque and then recited: "Have We not made the earth a receptacle," and since the grave is a kifat like the house, the one who stole from it had his hand cut off.

"Al-rawasi" (the firm ones) are the mountains, because they are anchored (rasat), that is, they are fixed. "Al-shamikh" is the high, lofty one, and from it comes "shamakha bi-anfihi," meaning he raised and exalted himself; the meaning is likened to a person. "Asqa" means he made it a source of irrigation for crops and benefits, while "saqa" means specifically for the lips (drinking). This is the view of a group of the people of lexicography, while others said both have one meaning. "Al-furat" is the pure, sweet one, and "furat" is not said of salty water. It is a term that gathers rainwater and river waters. The famous river is singled out with this for its honour: it is the river of Kufa. Sayhan is the river of Balkh, Jayhan is the Tigris, and the Nile is the river of Egypt. It is related from 'Ikrima that all water on earth is from these, but this is far-fetched. And Allah knows best.

It will be said to the worshippers of the cross: "Depart to the shadow of your deity, which is the cross, and it has three branches." Tashʿʿub (branching) means the division of a single body into separate parts. Then He negated from it the good qualities of shade.

The pronoun in "innahā" refers to Hell. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "bi-sharār" with an alif, the plural of sharāra (spark), and this is the dialect of Tamīm. "Al-qaṣr" in the words of Ibn ʿAbbās and a group of the exegetes is a noun of kind (ism nawʿ), meaning the palaces (al-quṣūr), which are the large dwellings built high. The Arabs have compared camels to them, and in this sense is the saying of al-Akhṭal:

"As if it were a Roman tower that Luzz built with plaster, bricks and stones."

Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) also said: "al-qaṣr" is also wood that was in the pre-Islamic period cut from large firewood of palm trees and others, of the length of a forearm, above it or below it, which people prepared for winter. It is called "al-qaṣr"; its singular is "qaṣra," and this is what is meant in the verse. It was called "al-qaṣṣār" because it surrounds the qaṣra. Mujāhid said: "al-qaṣr" means bundles of firewood, and this is the reading of the majority. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr also read "ka-l-quṣr" with a fatḥa on the ṣād, the plural of qaṣra, which means the necks of horses and camels, and likewise it is applied to people. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it means the roots of palm trees. Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan also read "ka-l-qiṣar" with a kasra on the qāf and a fatḥa on the ṣād, which is the plural of qaṣra like ḥalqa and ḥilaq (ring and rings) of iron.

The people differed concerning "al-jimālāt." The majority of exegetes said: it is the plural of "jimāl" on the sound pattern, like rijāl and rijālāt. Others said: by "ṣufr" they meant "black," and they recited the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts, their young are black like raisins."

The majority of people said: rather "ṣufr" means bright yellow, because it is more similar to the color of sparks, and they likened the sparks to the jimālāt. Al-Ḥasan read "ṣufur" with a ḍamma on the ṣād and the fāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Jubayr said: "al-jimālāt" are the cables of ships, which are the large ropes of ships, and when they are gathered in a circle, one against another, great masses come from them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "al-jimālāt" are large pieces of copper. The derivation of this was from the word "al-jumla" (the whole).

Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read "jimālatun" with a kasra on the jīm; the tāʾ is attached to jimāl to mark the feminine of the plural, so it is like ḥijr and ḥijāra. Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and al-Aʿmash read "jumālatun" with a ḍamma on the jīm. The rest of the seven readers, the majority, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) read "jimālātun" with a kasra on the jīm, as it is explained. Ibn ʿAbbās also, Qatāda, Ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan and Abū Rajāʾ (with a variant from them) read "jumālātun" with a ḍamma on the jīm. There is variation reported from Nāfiʿ, Abū Jaʿfar and Shayba. The ḍamma on the jīm in these is from "al-jumla" (the whole), not from "al-jumal," and the kasra is from "al-jimal" (camels), not from "al-jimla."

When He, may He be exalted, mentioned the deniers, He said, addressing Muḥammad (ﷺ): "This is a day when they will not speak." That is, the Day of Resurrection, in which awe and the humiliation of disbelief silence them. This is a specific station in which they do not speak, for the Qur'an has related their speech: "Our Lord, bring us out," and "Our Lord, cause us to die." So these are different stations. "Yawm" is in apposition to His saying "lā yanṭiqūna." Al-Aʿraj, al-Aʿmash and Abū Ḥaywa read "hādhā yawmun," and since it was attached to a non-declinable clause, he built it, so it is a fatḥa of construction (fatḥat bināʾ), and it is in the place of a nominative (rafʿ). It is possible that it is an adverbial of time (ẓarf), and the indication by "hādhā" would be to its throwing up sparks like the castle. His saying "fa-yaʿtadhirūn" is conjoined to "yuʾdhanu," and it was not put in the subjunctive as an answer to the negation, because of the similarity of the ends of the verses. Both possibilities are permissible.

His saying, may He be exalted: "This is the Day of Judgment; We have gathered you and the former peoples" is an address to the disbelievers on that day. "Al-awwalūn" (the former ones) referred to are the people of Noah and others among those who came at the beginning of the world and throughout the ages. Then He, may He be exalted, confronted His disbelieving servants, who deserve His punishment, with His saying: "So if you have a plan, then plot against Me." That is: if you have a trick or a scheme that will save you, then do it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 77, verse 41–50:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be among shades and springs.﴾ ﴿And fruit of whatever they desire.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers.﴾ ﴿"Eat and enjoy yourselves briefly; indeed, you are criminals."﴾ ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down.﴾ ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers.﴾ ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾

He, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of the righteous immediately after the condition of the people of the Fire, to show the difference. The "shades" (ẓilāl) in Paradise are an expression for the density of the trees and the excellence of the structures; otherwise there is no sun there that harms, such that a shade would be needed to protect from its heat. The majority read "fī ẓilālin" (in shades), while al-A'raj and al-A'mash read "fī ẓulalin" with a ḍammah on the ẓā'. "Al-'uyūn" (springs) are flowing water. His saying, exalted is He, "mimmā yashtahūn" (of whatever they desire) informs that eating and drinking there occur entirely according to their desires, unlike the situation in this world, where that is rare and exceptional. The custom is that a person restrains his desire to what his capacity requires. Here there is an omitted element indicated by the wording, its estimated meaning being: it will be said to them, "Eat." "Hanī'an" (with satisfaction) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and it is permissible that its accusative be on the basis of supplication. The kāf in His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed, We thus (kadhālika)" is the kāf of comparison, and the reference of "dhālika" is to what He mentioned of the bounties of the people of Paradise.

His saying, exalted is He, "Eat and enjoy yourselves" is addressed to Quraysh, in the sense: say to them, O Muhammad. This is an imperative form whose meaning is threat and warning, and His saying "qalīlan" (briefly) makes that clear. Then He, exalted is He, established the criminality that necessitates their punishment. Those who held that the whole surah is Meccan said: this verse concerns the disbelievers of Quraysh. Those who held that this verse among them is Medinan said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. Muqatil said: "It was revealed concerning Thaqīf, because they said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Remove the prayer from us, for we will not bow, as it is a disgrace.' But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused and said: 'There is no good in a religion that has no prayer in it.'"

His saying, exalted is He, "And when it is said to them, 'Bow down,' they do not bow down." It was said: this is a description of the condition of the hypocrites in the Hereafter, when the people prostrate and they wish to prostrate, but their spines turn to the ground and their vertebrae become like the cow's horns (ṣayāṣī al-baqar). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others. Qatada, along with others, said: this is the condition of the disbelievers of Quraysh in this world, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called them and they did not respond. The mention of bowing (rukū') is an expression for the whole prayer; this is the view of the majority. Some interpreters said: by bowing is meant humility, as the poet said:

﻿؎ ................ you see the hillocks in it prostrating before the hooves

that is, humbled. Qatada interpreted the verse as intending bowing itself, and said: "Upon you is goodness in bowing." What I say is: the mention of bowing here, and its singling out from among the rest of the states of worship, was because many of the Arabs were disdainful of bowing and prostration, and regarded them as a repugnant posture, because of the arrogance that was in their characters. Do you not see that one of them was asked, and it was said to him: "How do you say: 'istakhdha'tu' or 'istakhdhaytu'?" He said: "Both, I do not say." It was said to him: "Why?" He said: "Because the Arabs do not 'istakhdhī'." He thought he was being asked about the meaning, and did not understand that he was being asked about the word. In the book of biographies it is reported from some Arabs that he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, speaking on behalf of his people and himself, to excuse them from the prayer, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not answer him. It was said to him: "There is no escape from the prayer." Thereupon he said: "We will give it to you, even if it is a humiliation."

His saying, exalted is He, "So in what statement after this will they believe?" supports that the whole verse concerns Quraysh. The statement that the pronoun in "ba'dihi" (after it) refers to is the Qur'an. This is a warning and a rebuke. It is narrated from Ya'qub that he read "tu'minūn" with a tā' from above, in direct address, and it is also narrated from Ibn 'Amir.

The commentary of Surah [al-Mursalat] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

The commentary of Surah [al-Mursalat] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
